analysis.one_liner: Ends bulk collection of Americans' phone records and replaces it with case-by-case court orders.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in either committee it was sent to, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2013 revelations about the National Security Agency collecting nearly all Americans' phone call records in bulk, Rep. Adam Schiff proposed a reform: amend the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act so the FBI could no longer use the 'business records' provision to demand bulk call data. Instead, the FBI would have to show a judge a specific record tied to a specific foreign terrorist organization or intelligence activity before ordering a phone company to search and hand over results. The bill set a 12-hour deadline for carriers to comply, created an emergency path where the FBI could act first and get a judge's approval within five days, required records about Americans to be destroyed after five years unless a judge found probable cause of a crime, and ordered annual public reporting on how often these searches happened.
analysis.who_benefits: Every American with a phone. The bill would have taken away the legal basis for searching phone records in bulk and replaced it with a judge-approved, record-by-record process, with destruction requirements for data on U.S. persons kept beyond five years without a probable-cause finding.

how_it_helps.text: Removes call data records from the 'business records' category the FBI could use to obtain bulk production orders, ending the legal foundation for indiscriminate collection of phone metadata [S2] [S3].

Requires a FISA judge to approve any search of call records based on specific facts tying the record to a particular foreign terrorist organization, intelligence activity, or foreign power — a targeted, individualized process instead of bulk searches [S2] [S3].

Caps federal retention of call records about U.S. persons at five years unless a FISA judge finds probable cause the records are evidence of a crime, and requires destruction of records obtained under an emergency directive if a court later denies approval [S2] [S3].

Requires the FBI to report publicly each year how many searches were conducted, how many involved U.S. phone numbers, how often emergency directives were used, and how often courts rejected applications [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Telecommunications carriers, who would be compelled to run searches and produce results on short deadlines (compensated at prevailing rates with public funds), and the FBI, which would lose the convenience of querying a single bulk database and would operate under tighter court oversight and public reporting.

drawbacks.text: The bill preserves an emergency path allowing the FBI to direct phone companies to search records without any court order first, with judicial review only after the fact (notification within 24 hours, application within five days) [S2] [S3].

The standard for a court order is 'reasonable suspicion' based on specific facts — lower than the probable-cause standard required for ordinary criminal warrants — and the bill includes a presumption that a record is fair game if it merely pertains to someone 'in contact with' a suspected agent of a foreign power [S3].
It bars anyone from disclosing that the FBI sought or obtained call records, and it requires taxpayers to compensate carriers at prevailing rates for complying [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the trade is favorable: it eliminates bulk searches of Americans' call records and adds court oversight, retention limits, and annual public reporting, while keeping a fast emergency tool for genuine ticking-clock cases. The honest costs are the warrant-less emergency directive, a lower-than-warrant standard of proof, and continued secrecy around each individual order.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Judiciary and Intelligence committees, then sent to a Judiciary subcommittee in March 2014, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the Telephone Metadata Reform Act on January 14, 2014, with no cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].

The bill was referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, so both would have to act on the parts within their jurisdiction [S3] [S5].

On March 20, 2014, the House referred the bill to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations; the record shows no further action, hearing, markup, or vote for the remainder of the 113th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The intelligence community and the existing bulk phone-records program are better off, because the bill that would have replaced bulk collection with individualized court orders died without ever being considered. Phone carriers are also better off, avoiding compelled search-and-production duties on tight deadlines.

for.name: Rep. Adam Schiff
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA); member of the House Intelligence Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; referred it to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations and took no further action
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill

against.name: House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence
against.role: Second committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after the referral

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors of either party, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill locks phone companies in as the government's permanent search mechanism: every query of call records would run through the carriers, who must comply within 12 (or in emergencies, 6) hours and are compensated at taxpayer expense. Carriers avoid the reputational exposure of handing over bulk databases, but gain a compulsory, paid role in surveillance of their own customers.

The bill would end the legal basis for bulk call-records collection under the FISA business-records provision and require individualized court-approved searches, retention limits, and annual public reporting — a direct constraint on agency practice.
